comparator.name: Econometrics and Operations Research
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 SBE regulations and current study outline confirm a 180 EC degree. The first two years each contain eight compulsory 6.5 EC courses and two 4 EC skills trainings. Year three includes 26 EC abroad, one restricted skill, two restricted disciplinary courses, one approved elective and a 10.5 EC thesis. The programme has no formal specialisations. The outline preserves the official options.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI

core: Econometrics and operations research as the two defining fields of the programme, combining mathematical modelling with economic and managerial questions
Mathematical foundations and rigorous mathematical reasoning: Analysis I and II, Linear Algebra and the calculus and linear-algebra tools that support the quantitative curriculum

Probability, mathematical statistics and econometric methods, including Probability Theory, Mathematical Statistics and Econometric Methods I, used to model uncertainty and data and to predict economic and business trends
Optimisation and operations research: Optimisation and Operations Research, formulating and solving optimisation problems under constraints and making organisations and systems more efficient

Economic theory and finance as the substantive context of the quantitative work: Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Finance, Macroeconomics and Finance, Game Theory and Economics and Economics of Uncertainty and Information
Programming, algorithms and software used to implement quantitative models, including Programming and, in the elective range, Advanced Algorithms and software for econometrics or operations research
Independent quantitative research and research skills: the Bachelor's thesis, the second-year projects and the Philosophy of Science and Responsible Econometrics skills courses
adjacent: Applied econometrics for finance and markets: finance and financial risk, and marketing, as recurring application fields for econometric analysis
Advanced elective directions attached to year 3 in the curriculum page: advanced econometric methods, auctions and electronic-market design, advanced algorithms and actuarial mathematics
questions: How can statistical models and data be used to forecast and predict economic and business developments?
How can decisions in complex organisations and systems be made more efficient through mathematical optimisation?

trace: teaches Python programming, structured and object-oriented problem solving and elements of discrete mathematics; it directly implements the Programming component and the programming and algorithms used to build quantitative models

introduces microeconomics (supply and demand, game theory, consumer behaviour, the firm, market structure) and macroeconomics; it directly implements the economic-theory foundation and the game-theory element of Game Theory and Economics

covers logic, discrete structures and the mathematics of decision-making with applications to algorithm construction; it makes a specific contribution to the rigorous mathematical reasoning and proof skills the target emphasises, though not the analysis proofs themselves
teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations with projects in economics and other sciences; it directly implements the calculus content of Analysis I

introduces research design and descriptive and inferential statistics including analysis of variance; it makes a specific contribution to the statistical inference part of Mathematical Statistics and is the formal prerequisite for UCR's Econometrics and economics courses
Applies search, continuous and discrete optimisation, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and adversarial decision methods.
teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation and an own data-analysis project; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the applied data work behind econometric analysis
covers systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces, linear transformations and determinants; it directly implements the Linear Algebra foundation used by regression and optimisation

covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly implements Probability Theory and the estimation part of Mathematical Statistics
studies national income, growth, inflation, unemployment, business cycles, fiscal and monetary policy and international trade; it directly implements Macroeconomics
Develops algorithm analysis, graph traversal, shortest paths and minimum spanning trees, including selected methods used in operations research.

treats numerical solution of equations, optimisation and differential-equation problems that lack analytic solutions; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the computational side of the mathematical and optimisation work, although it is not an econometrics course
Examines advanced algorithmic complexity, arithmetic, factorisation and fast matrix multiplication.

covers consumer choice under uncertainty, market structures, strategic behaviour and general equilibrium; it directly implements Microeconomics and part of the economics of uncertainty and strategic behaviour
Builds neural networks for prediction, image and text tasks. These methods overlap Maastricht’s optional deep learning course.

covers multivariate statistical models, regression analysis, logistic regression and non-parametric tests; it directly contributes the regression modelling that underlies Econometric Methods, although its examples come from the behavioural sciences

covers linear regression, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods and other modelling and prediction techniques; it directly contributes prediction and forecasting methods and complements classical econometric estimation
Develops financial reporting, costing, cash-flow interpretation and corporate finance decisions.
Uses Bayesian networks and Markov decision processes to analyse choices under uncertainty and partial observability.
extends calculus to several variables and differential equations using computer algebra; it directly implements the multivariable content of Analysis II
teaches OLS, generalised least squares and instrumental-variables estimators, t-, F- and LM-tests, Monte Carlo simulation and an empirical paper; it directly implements Econometric Methods I

studies how biases, heuristics and framing shape decisions under uncertainty using experiments; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the economics of uncertainty and decision-making, though it is behavioural rather than expected-utility economics

covers reinforcement learning as sequential decision optimisation with implemented agents; it makes a specific complementary contribution to dynamic optimisation, although it is formulated as machine learning rather than as operations research
Develops the business and entrepreneurial foundation for subsequent financial and market research courses.
Examines banking, financial markets, bond, stock and derivative pricing, interest-rate risk and financial intermediation.
Uses practical market research to plan data collection, analyse consumer information and present findings.

studies consumer behaviour, marketing strategy and digital and AI-driven marketing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the marketing application field in which econometric analysis is applied, though it is not itself quantitative

analyses the impact of AI on competitiveness, labour markets, economic growth and inequality; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the economic and business context of forecasting trends, but it is a non-technical course

analyses market failure, externalities, taxation, public spending and the empirical economic impact of policy; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the economics of markets and information through applied economic evidence
introduces relational databases, SQL and query processing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to handling the financial and market data that applied empirical work draws on

alternatives.label: Mathematics, econometrics and optimisation
alternatives.labelReason: Mathematics, statistics and economics support econometric modelling, while algorithms, linear programming and AI decision methods address optimisation. These courses make up a quantitative composition with substantive operations-research overlap.
alternatives.concept: Use calculus, linear algebra, probability and econometrics to analyse economic data. Study linear programming, graph algorithms and decision-making under uncertainty to model how systems can work more efficiently.
progression: Programming precedes algorithms and advanced AI. Mathematical Methods precedes Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics and later mathematical study. Data Science precedes machine learning, and statistics precedes econometrics.

alternatives.label: Econometrics, finance and market analysis
alternatives.labelReason: Econometrics and quantitative methods support a coherent applied option in financial markets, consumer behaviour and market research. Finance and market research receive more weight than mathematical optimisation.
alternatives.concept: Use statistics, econometrics and computing to study financial and market questions. Combine banking and asset pricing with consumer behaviour and practical market research to understand how firms and investors make decisions.
alternatives.distinctness: Seven courses differ in each direction. This option adds finance, marketing, market research, public economics, business AI, business foundations and databases. The closest option gives those places to advanced calculus, numerical methods, logic, algorithms and optimisation.
progression: Business foundations precede market research and finance. Mathematical Methods precedes Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics and deep learning. Introductory data handling precedes machine learning, and statistics precedes econometrics.

candidates.label: Applied econometrics for finance and marketing analytics

selection.assessment: Two options cover the programme’s quantitative core and its finance and marketing applications. They share 17 courses and differ by seven in each direction. The remaining interests support these options or describe topics and outcomes within them.

blocks: Both study differentiation in one variable. Maastricht combines this with mathematical reasoning and sequences.
Linear Algebra covers matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations, the same subject as the target's Linear Algebra.
Both cover multivariable calculus and differential equations. Maastricht gives more attention to rigorous analysis and constrained optimisation.
Probability & Statistics teaches probability theory and distributions, the primary subject of Probability Theory; it adds estimation that belongs to Mathematical Statistics.
Both develop statistical inference and estimation. UCR focuses on applied experimental designs and regression, while Maastricht develops the mathematical theory.
Both study regression estimation, hypothesis testing and economic data. UCR includes instrumental variables and an empirical paper. Maastricht also teaches time-series models and uses R and EViews.
Introduction to Programming teaches Python programming and problem solving, the subject of the target's Programming component.
Both study linear programming and optimisation. UCR places these alongside search and constraint methods, while Maastricht teaches simplex methods, duality and nonlinear programming in greater depth.
Both study graph algorithms, including shortest paths and spanning trees. Maastricht also covers network flows, stochastic processes and queues.
Introduction to Economics covers game theory and market structure in its microeconomics part, an identifiable part of Game Theory and Economics; UCR has no dedicated game-theory course.
Microeconomics & Behavior covers consumer choice, market structures and strategic behaviour, the subject of Microeconomics at a more advanced level.
International Macroeconomics covers national income, growth, inflation and policy, the same subject as Macroeconomics.
Both study risk and return and price bonds and stocks. UCR also covers banking and derivatives. This course appears in the finance option.
The UCR options distribute relevant study between macroeconomics and finance. Maastricht combines exchange-rate modelling and international finance in one course.
Maastricht uses mathematical models for operations and marketing. UCR studies related tools across its research methods, optimisation and market courses.
UCR studies behavioural and computational approaches to uncertainty. Maastricht develops formal microeconomic models of risk and information.
Academic skills, projects, study abroad and thesis
Maastricht has a dedicated Philosophy of Science skills course.
Maastricht has a dedicated course on ethical, social and practical issues in econometrics.
Maastricht combines optimisation, game theory and programming in a team project with reports and a presentation.
Maastricht assesses a practical case integrating operations research and econometrics through a paper and presentation.
The comparator includes a required period at a partner university.
Students choose one of two disciplinary software courses. UCR provides general programming and data methods in separate courses.
Maastricht requires a supervised individual paper. UCR displays optional independent research alongside it.
Year-three disciplinary courses and elective space
One of two course choices from the four-course disciplinary list.
The second choice from the four-course disciplinary list. UCR offers related algorithms and deep learning in the mathematical option.
Students choose from the programme elective list.

notes.text: UCR covers linear programming, graph algorithms, regression, and decision-making under uncertainty. Maastricht develops operations research and econometric modelling through dedicated courses and integrated projects. It also offers specialist study in game theory, information economics and advanced econometrics.
Maastricht requires a 26 EC study-abroad period and a 10.5 EC individual thesis. UCR offers optional independent research in addition to the courses shown.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht Econometrics and Operations Research uses mathematics, statistics and economics to model decisions and analyse data. The first two years build foundations and include integrated projects. The final year combines study abroad, selected disciplinary work and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: One UCR option focuses on mathematics, econometrics and optimisation. The other uses quantitative methods to study finance and markets. Maastricht has a longer sequence in mathematical modelling and operations research, with dedicated team projects and a required thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The third-year skills training, two disciplinary courses and elective remain choices from official lists.

componentNotes.y3-01: Apply after earning at least 53.5 first-year EC and complete all 60 first-year EC before departure. The credits abroad require approval.
componentNotes.y3-02: Choose Introduction to Software in Econometrics or Introduction to Software in Operations Research.
componentNotes.y3-03: Choose two different courses from Econometric Methods II, Advanced Algorithms, Deep Learning for (Un)structured Data, and Market Design.
componentNotes.y3-05: Choose one 6.5 EC course from the programme’s approved elective list.
componentNotes.y3-06: The individual 10.5 EC thesis is normally written in semester six.
